newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iraq developing missiles, U.S. mulls strike - paper.
newsitem.headline: Iraq developing missiles, U.S. mulls strike - paper.

text.p: A German newspaper reported on Tuesday that United Nations inspectors have discovered Iraq has continued to develop missiles in contravention of U.N. resolutions and said the United States was contemplating a possible missile strike against Iraq.

In an advance release from Wednesday's edition, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) said the United States could make a decision this week on whether to launch a Tomahawk missile strike at Iraq.
It sourced its report to "American security sources" and said the American Central Intelligence Agency had told Washington about the latest reports on Monday.

The FAZ said U.N. inspectors who were in Iraq between January 5 and 23 had found evidence, according to American sources, that Iraq was continuing to develop missiles with a range of around 1,600 km (1,000 miles).
Iraq was banned from such weapons programmes under U.N. resolutions passed after a U.S.-led multinational force drove its invading forces out of Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.
Sanctions imposed as a result of the Gulf War have been partially eased in the last few months, and Iraq has been allowed to resume strictly limited oil exports.
Evidence gathered by U.N. inspectors showed that Iraqi engineers had worked on a secret long-range missile programme between July and September 1992, the FAZ said.
It said there was no direct proof that the work had still been going on in recent months, but said it was nevertheless "highly probable".

It said American computer experts had located on Iraqi computer disks a German software simulation which Iraqi engineers had used to test trajectories for a modified Scud missile with a theoretical range of 1,586 km (985 miles).
The newspaper said Washington had undertaken to inform its allies in advance -- particularly Britain and France -- if it decided to launch new missile strikes on targets in Iraq.
The FAZ also said U.N. inspectors had been "massively obstructed" during their recent visit.
It said chief inspector Rolf Ekeus had written to Iraqi Prime Minister Tariq Aziz on January 13 telling him that Iraq was contravening U.N. resolutions and this would have consequences.
